The HIV care register and pre-ART register are used to track the number of individuals newly enrolled in HIV treatment or initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) during a specific reporting period. 2. The indicator 10N measures the number of HIV-positive women of reproductive age (15–49 years) attending HIV care and treatment services who have an unmet need for family planning. This helps assess whether family planning services are adequately addressing the prevention of unintended pregnancies among HIV-positive women (Prong 2). 3. The global indicator 111 2.18N captures the number of HIV-positive individuals enrolled in HIV care (pre-ART or ART) in the past 12 months whose tuberculosis (TB) status was assessed and documented during their last visit within the reporting period. This reflects the implementation of the recommendation to screen people living with HIV for TB at diagnosis and during every follow-up visit. 4. Indicators to monitor the entire cascade of intensive TB case finding are outlined in the WHO TB/HIV Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) guide. 5. The indicator 11N tracks the number of adults receiving HIV care in the past 12 months whose sexual partner’s HIV status is documented in their clinical records. This data can be collected during annual reviews at all facilities or sentinel sites. It measures the program’s ability to identify and test the sexual partners of people living with HIV, aiming to prevent ongoing transmission among sero-discordant couples and enroll HIV-positive partners into care. 6. Program records, pre-ART and ART registers, and laboratory records are used to measure the uptake of cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis, a critical component of quality care for eligible individuals in HIV care. In many settings, key population-specific data cannot be collected through routine program monitoring, necessitating surveys. 7. The number and percentage of people living with HIV who are eligible for ART but have not started ART are tracked. This indicator provides insight into the size of the ART waitlist in settings where patients visit facilities but cannot initiate ART. It also demonstrates the presence of a system to track individuals eligible for but not yet on ART. 8. ART registers and HIV testing registers ideally collect data routinely on all children, especially in settings with electronic patient data systems. This measures the efficiency of program linkages between diagnosis and treatment among HIV-positive children, all of whom are eligible for immediate ART regardless of CD4 count. 9. Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV, even in the era of ART scale-up. In 2013, 3% of the estimated 35 million people living with HIV developed TB, and one-quarter of all HIV-related deaths were attributed to TB. Early initiation of ART, regardless of CD4 count, is crucial for individuals with HIV and active TB to reduce mortality. 10. National TB and AIDS control programs must collaborate to ensure joint services are available. WHO published its policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities in 2012, emphasizing the importance of integrated services for TB/HIV co-infection. 11. The cascade of services for TB/HIV co-infection depends on whether a person enters through the HIV care system or the TB system. Individuals diagnosed with HIV should be tested for TB, and those diagnosed with TB should be tested for HIV. Understanding this cascade helps identify opportunities to improve service provision and reduce losses to follow-up. 12. Recent developments in TB/HIV include progress in collaborative activities, such as high coverage of HIV testing among TB patients, TB screening among people living with HIV, and ART initiation among HIV-positive TB patients. Research highlights the effectiveness of early ART and isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in preventing HIV-associated TB and reducing mortality. 13. WHO recommends the use of Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial diagnostic test for TB among individuals suspected of having HIV-associated TB. This test detects both drug-sensitive and rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis from sputum specimens in under two hours, offering greater sensitivity and specificity than conventional sputum microscopy. 14. The 2011 Political Declaration on HIV/AIDS endorsed by United Nations Member States provided momentum for implementing collaborative TB/HIV activities. Efforts are now focused on tracking HIV-associated TB deaths and improving estimates of TB burden and mortality. 15. TB among children and women has received increased attention, including strategies for screening and diagnosing TB in maternal, neonatal, and child health settings. 16. The 2015 revision of the WHO guide to monitoring and evaluating collaborative TB/HIV activities emphasizes measuring patient outcomes, program quality, and impact. It reduces the number of global-level indicators from 13 to seven and introduces new indicators to monitor intensified TB case finding, access to rapid TB diagnostic tests, early ART, and treatment compliance for latent TB infection. 17. Data required to track collaborative TB/HIV activities are collected by national TB and HIV programs using different databases. Discrepancies often arise due to differing indicator definitions and reporting timeframes. TB data are typically reported quarterly and are not cumulative, while HIV data may be annual and cumulative. 18. Reporting on TB/HIV indicators is often inconsistent and incomplete. Some countries fail to report key indicators, such as IPT coverage, or provide numerator data without corresponding denominators, making coverage measurement impossible. 19. The 2015 revision of the TB/HIV monitoring and evaluation guide offers greater clarity for these measurements, emphasizing the importance of monitoring the entire cascade of care from screening and testing to treatment for people co-infected with HIV and TB. 20. WHO, UNODC, and UNAIDS have developed guidance for special populations at elevated risk for HIV and TB or requiring specific service delivery considerations. These include consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations and policy guidelines for managing TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis in people who inject drugs. 21. Measuring the risk of TB among healthcare workers relative to the general population is a recommended core global and national indicator. This serves as a proxy for the impact of infection control activities in healthcare facilities. 22. The prevalence of active TB disease among people living with HIV who are newly enrolled in HIV care is measured to assess the burden of TB and the effectiveness of efforts to detect HIV-associated TB. Early detection enables prompt TB treatment and early ART initiation. 23. The extent to which HIV-positive TB patients receive ART during TB treatment is measured. High coverage indicates strong collaboration between national HIV and TB programs, as both treatments are necessary to minimize mortality. 24. The extent to which individuals newly enrolled in HIV care are started on treatment for latent TB infection (LTBI) is measured. Treating LTBI reduces the burden of TB among people living with HIV.
